finalAnswer: Write the number of valid single folds to folding.out.
shortExplanation: Use twice the fold position as an integer. Every knot in the overlapping strands must have its reflected partner.
detailedSteps: Let the fold position be $f$. A knot at $x$ reflects to $2f-x$. It needs a matching knot only when the reflected position lies in $[0,L]$; otherwise it belongs to the unmatched longer tail.

The shorter strand has an endpoint knot. If the left side is shorter, its endpoint at 0 reflects to $2f$; if the right side is shorter, its endpoint at $L$ reflects to $2f-L$. The matching knot is at an integer position, so $q=2f$ must be an integer.
Try every integer $q$ from 1 through $2L-1$. These are all possible valid folds, including half-integer folds, and exclude both rope endpoints.
Sort the knots. For each candidate and each knot $x$, compute $q-x$. When that value is within the rope, require it to occur in the sorted list. Use binary search and exact integers.

If all required partners exist, every knot in either overlapping strand has its counterpart. This proves the candidate is valid. A knot at the fold matches itself; knots beyond the overlap impose no requirement.

Sorting takes $O(N\log N)$ time. At most $2L-1$ candidates each make at most $N$ binary searches, so total time is $O(N\log N+LN\log N)$ and memory is $O(N)$. With the actual bounds there are at most 1,999,900 membership checks.
Use folding.in and folding.out. The input includes distinct knots at both endpoints, and their order may be arbitrary. Doubled coordinates avoid rounding and fit int under the original bounds.
keyIdeas: Endpoint alignment makes doubled fold positions integral.
Test only the overlapping strands, preserving the longer tail.
Exact reflection and binary search prove each candidate.
commonMistakes: Counting folds at the rope endpoints.
Requiring every knot in the longer tail to match.
Testing only integer fold positions and missing half-integers.
difficultyNotes: The main argument is why every valid real fold lies on a half-integer grid and how overlap changes the matching condition.

finalAnswer: Write the union area of the rectangles to planting.out.
shortExplanation: Split the plane at all rectangle boundaries. Add each resulting cell once if any rectangle covers it.
detailedSteps: Collect both x boundaries and both y boundaries from every rectangle. Sort each list and remove duplicates. The implementation expresses each rectangle using its left, right, bottom and top bounds.

Consecutive x boundaries and consecutive y boundaries define elementary cells. No original rectangle boundary passes through a cell interior, so a rectangle covers the whole cell or none of its interior.
For each cell, check all rectangles. It is covered when its two x boundaries and two y boundaries lie inside one rectangle. Stop at the first covering rectangle.
Add width times height for a covered cell. Cells have disjoint interiors, so overlap is counted once. Shared edges have zero area and do not affect the answer.
There are at most $(2N-1)^2$ cells, and each checks at most $N$ rectangles. The running time is $O(N^3)$ and storage is $O(N)$; no large coordinate-range grid is built.

All grass lies within a 20,000 by 20,000 box under the actual coordinate limits. The answer is at most 400,000,000. Use a long long multiplication and sum for clear, safe arithmetic; the real bound itself also fits signed int.
Use planting.in and planting.out. This is the Bronze problem with at most ten rectangles. Containment, crossing overlap and touching edges all follow the same cell argument.
keyIdeas: A covered cell contributes once regardless of overlap count.
commonMistakes: Adding individual rectangle areas without removing overlap.
Allocating a board for every possible coordinate.
Using the Silver constraints for this Bronze task.
difficultyNotes: A correct partition argument turns the geometric union into a small exact enumeration under the Bronze bound.

finalAnswer: Write the requested character, m or o, to moo.out.
shortExplanation: Store sequence lengths, then locate the requested position in the left copy, middle block or right copy.
detailedSteps: Let $\ell_k$ be the length of $S(k)$. The base is $\ell_0=3$, and the middle block at level $k$ has length $k+3$. Therefore $\ell_k=2\ell_{k-1}+k+3$. Grow the length table until it reaches the requested one-based position.
Every sequence starts with the previous one, so this finite sequence contains the same requested character as the infinite sequence.
At level $k>0$, let $p=\ell_{k-1}$. Positions 1 through $p$ belong to the left copy; descend one level without changing the position.
Positions $p+1$ through $p+k+3$ belong to the middle block. Its first character is m and every other character is o, so answer directly there.
For a position farther right, subtract $p+k+3$ and descend into the right copy. Each branch preserves the requested character as a local one-based position in the smaller sequence.
Eventually reach the base sequence moo: position 1 is m, and positions 2 and 3 are o. Do not confuse a zero-based string index with the one-based input.

Lengths at least double, so building the table and descending take $O(\log N)$ time and $O(\log N)$ memory. At the actual maximum, level 27 suffices with length 1,073,741,792. Use long long lengths and positions, and historical files moo.in and moo.out.
keyIdeas: Length growth avoids building the enormous sequence.
Three block intervals cover each level without gaps.
Adjust the position only when entering the right copy.
commonMistakes: Subtracting an offset while descending into the left copy.
Mixing one-based input with zero-based indexing.
difficultyNotes: Careful interval boundaries and a position-preserving descent are the essential parts of the recursive lookup.
